subtopic_detail: Volume expansion with albumin before committing to a diagnosis of hepatorenal syndrome
stem:
You are the medical registrar looking after a 55 year old woman with alcohol related cirrhosis and diuretic responsive ascites, admitted five days ago for symptom control. Her creatinine has climbed steadily since admission.

She has passed less urine than usual but has no urinary symptoms and no rash. Her spironolactone and frusemide were withheld 48 hours ago and she has had no contrast, no non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and no aminoglycosides. A diagnostic paracentesis on admission showed a polymorphonuclear count of 60 x10^6/L. Renal tract ultrasound shows normal sized unobstructed kidneys.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 94/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 186 micromol/L (45-90), admission creatinine 88 micromol/L, sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), bilirubin 78 micromol/L (2-24), international normalised ratio 1.9 (0.8-1.2)
data_table.Urine: Urinary sodium 8 mmol/L, no protein on dipstick, microscopy shows no casts and no red cells

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give intravenous albumin daily for two days with diuretics withheld
options.rationale: A low urinary sodium and bland sediment are shared by both prerenal azotaemia and hepatorenal syndrome, so neither can be diagnosed on those findings; the defining step is failure of the creatinine to improve after diuretic withdrawal plus albumin volume expansion at 1 g/kg daily for two days (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis).
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.text: Start terlipressin with noradrenaline in the intensive care unit
options.rationale: Vasoconstrictor therapy is reserved for hepatorenal syndrome that persists after the albumin challenge, and committing to it now would treat a diagnosis that has not yet been earned (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

options.text: Give a two litre bolus of 0.9 per cent sodium chloride over four hours
options.rationale: Crystalloid does not hold in the intravascular space when the albumin is low and portal pressure is high, so it worsens ascites and peripheral oedema while doing less than albumin to restore effective arterial volume (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis).
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.text: Start low dose dopamine and repeat the creatinine in 24 hours
options.rationale: Renal dose dopamine has repeatedly failed to prevent or reverse acute kidney injury in randomised trials and adds arrhythmia risk without altering the course (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange urgent renal biopsy before any volume expansion is given
options.rationale: Biopsy is the near pair when there is proteinuria, haematuria or casts pointing to an intrinsic glomerular lesion, but the sediment here is bland and the coagulopathy makes biopsy hazardous (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

explanation.summary: Acute kidney injury in cirrhosis has four common causes: prerenal from diuretics or bleeding, acute tubular necrosis, hepatorenal syndrome and post renal obstruction. The diagnosis of hepatorenal syndrome is one of exclusion and requires no improvement after two days off diuretics with albumin expansion, absence of shock, no recent nephrotoxin, and no parenchymal disease on urinalysis and ultrasound. This sequence matters because vasoconstrictor therapy is costly and carries ischaemic risk, while a patient who is simply over diuresed recovers with volume alone. Any patient reaching a confirmed diagnosis should be assessed for liver transplantation at the same time as vasoconstrictor therapy is started.
key_points: Urinary sodium below 20 mmol/L cannot distinguish prerenal azotaemia from hepatorenal syndrome; both avidly retain sodium.
Diuretic withdrawal plus albumin 1 g/kg daily for two days is the diagnostic challenge.
Bland urinary sediment argues against acute tubular necrosis and against glomerular disease.
Terlipressin with albumin is the treatment only after the challenge has failed.
Transplant assessment runs in parallel with medical treatment.
explanation.pearls: Albumin for the diagnostic challenge is capped at 100 g per day, because volumes beyond that give no additional expansion and precipitate pulmonary oedema in a patient whose oncotic gradient is already deranged.

sources.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis

subtopic_detail: Choosing manometry after a normal endoscopy in progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar seeing a 42 year old man in clinic. For eight months food has felt like it sticks behind his breastbone, and he now has the same trouble with water. He has taken to standing up and arching his back to get things down.

He wakes at night coughing and finds bits of the previous evening's meal on the pillow, still tasting of the meal rather than sour. He has lost 6 kg. A gastroscopy last week showed retained saliva and food residue in the oesophagus with normal mucosa, and the endoscope passed into the stomach with slight resistance at the junction. Biopsies from the mid and distal oesophagus showed no eosinophils and no inflammation.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), albumin 38 g/L (35-50), C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange a therapeutic trial of high dose proton pump inhibitor
options.rationale: An empirical acid suppression trial delays diagnosis in a man who has already lost 6 kg, and the biopsies have already excluded the eosinophilic oesophagitis that such a trial would be testing for (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

options.text: Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to define motility
options.rationale: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset with regurgitation of undigested food and a normal mucosa is a motility problem, and manometry is the test that both confirms failed lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation and assigns the subtype that determines whether dilatation, myotomy or peroral endoscopic myotomy is offered (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia).

options.text: Arrange a barium swallow with a timed five minute upright film
options.rationale: A timed barium study is a useful adjunct for measuring emptying before and after treatment, but it cannot assign the motility subtype and a normal study does not exclude the diagnosis (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia).

options.text: Arrange 24 hour ambulatory oesophageal pH and impedance monitoring
options.rationale: Reflux monitoring answers a different question, and the regurgitated material here tastes of the meal rather than being acidic, which points away from acid reflux as the mechanism (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia).

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the chest and upper abdomen
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging is the near pair and is reserved for suspected malignancy at the junction, suggested by onset after 55 years, a history of under six months and rapid weight loss, a pattern this man does not fit (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Achalasia).

explanation.summary: Dysphagia that involves liquids as early as solids points to a motility disorder, whereas dysphagia that begins with solids and progresses to liquids points to a structural narrowing. Endoscopy still comes first in every case, both to exclude mucosal disease and to take biopsies, but a normal endoscopy does not end the workup. High resolution manometry defines the three treatment relevant subtypes, and the response to pneumatic dilatation and myotomy differs sharply between them. Untreated disease leads to progressive oesophageal dilatation, aspiration pneumonia and a small long term risk of squamous carcinoma.
key_points: Simultaneous solid and liquid dysphagia suggests a motility disorder rather than a stricture.
Regurgitation of undigested, non acidic food and nocturnal cough are characteristic.
Endoscopy is done first but a normal result does not exclude the diagnosis.
High resolution manometry confirms the diagnosis and assigns the subtype that guides therapy.
Malignancy at the junction can mimic the picture and is suspected with older age, short history and marked weight loss.
explanation.pearls: The endoscopic finding of retained food or saliva in an oesophagus with normal mucosa has a very high positive predictive value for a motility disorder, and its absence is why endoscopy alone misses roughly a third of cases.

subtopic_detail: Malignancy screening at diagnosis of an inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin disease
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 54 year old woman referred with three months of difficulty lifting her arms above her head to hang out washing and trouble rising from a low chair without pushing up on her thighs.

She has noticed a purple discolouration around both eyelids that she first blamed on a new eye cream, and scaly raised patches over the backs of her knuckles. There is no ptosis, no double vision and no fatigability on sustained upgaze. Muscle power is 3 out of 5 at the shoulder and hip girdles with normal distal power, and reflexes are preserved throughout. She takes no statin and no other regular medication.

data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 1840 U/L (30-150), alanine aminotransferase 84 U/L (5-35), C reactive protein 9 mg/L (less than 5), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), antinuclear antibody positive at 1 in 320

lead_in: In addition to starting oral prednisolone, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of both thighs with muscle biopsy
options.rationale: Imaging guided biopsy confirms the inflammatory nature of the myopathy and is often done, but it does not address the malignancy association that changes this woman's prognosis and management most (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

options.text: Electromyography of the proximal limbs with nerve conduction study
options.rationale: Electrophysiology separates myopathic from neurogenic weakness, but the raised creatine kinase with preserved reflexes and normal distal power has already made that distinction (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Dermatomyositis).

options.text: Serum thyroid stimulating hormone with a vitamin D concentration
options.rationale: Hypothyroid and osteomalacic myopathy are reasonable considerations in proximal weakness, but the thyroid function is already normal and neither produces a creatine kinase in the thousands with a photodistributed rash (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Dermatomyositis).

options.text: Skin biopsy of the knuckle plaques with direct immunofluorescence
options.rationale: The near pair here is cutaneous lupus, which shares an interface dermatitis on histology, but lupus rash spares the knuckles and involves the skin between them, so a biopsy would not change management (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists).

options.text: Computed tomography of chest, abdomen and pelvis with mammography
options.rationale: The combination of proximal myopathy with the periorbital and knuckle skin changes carries a several fold increase in occult malignancy, concentrated in the three years around diagnosis, so cross sectional imaging with age and sex appropriate screening is performed at presentation rather than deferred (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

explanation.summary: An inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin disease is one of the few rheumatological diagnoses that mandates a malignancy hunt at presentation, since the association is strongest in adults over 45 and in the first three years after diagnosis. Ovarian, lung, breast, colorectal, pancreatic and gastric cancers are over represented, and in some populations nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Antibody testing helps stratify this risk further, with certain myositis specific antibodies conferring high malignancy risk and others associating instead with interstitial lung disease. Screening for interstitial lung disease with high resolution imaging and lung function, and swallow assessment for pharyngeal weakness, run alongside the malignancy search.
key_points: Adult onset inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin disease carries a several fold malignancy risk.
Risk concentrates in the three years around diagnosis and rises with age above 45.
Cross sectional imaging plus age and sex appropriate screening is done at presentation.
Myositis specific antibodies stratify risk of malignancy versus interstitial lung disease.
Interstitial lung disease and pharyngeal weakness are the other two assessments due at diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Anti transcription intermediary factor 1 gamma antibody in an adult carries a malignancy risk approaching one in two, while anti melanoma differentiation associated gene 5 antibody instead flags rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease with a near normal creatine kinase.

subtopic_detail: Securing histology before treatment in superior vena caval obstruction without airway compromise
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 66 year old man who has smoked 30 cigarettes a day since his twenties. For three weeks his face has felt puffy, worst when he first wakes, and his shirt collar no longer does up.

He has no stridor, speaks in full sentences and lies flat without distress. There are distended veins across the upper chest and neck that do not pulsate, and his face is plethoric. He has had no previous cancer and no biopsy of any kind. A computed tomography scan shows a right hilar mass compressing the superior vena cava with collateral filling, mediastinal nodes, and no cerebral oedema.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), lactate dehydrogenase 310 U/L (120-250)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent biopsy of the mediastinal mass for tissue diagnosis
options.rationale: Without airway compromise or cerebral oedema there is time to obtain histology, and histology determines everything that follows because small cell carcinoma and lymphoma respond to systemic therapy while non small cell disease is treated with radiotherapy or a stent (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

options.text: Start high dose dexamethasone and arrange biopsy in one week
options.rationale: Corticosteroid given before biopsy can lyse lymphoma cells and render the specimen non diagnostic, which is why it is held back unless there is airway or cerebral compromise (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online).

options.text: Refer for endovascular stenting of the superior vena cava today
options.rationale: Stenting gives the fastest symptom relief and is the right move for severe or life threatening obstruction, but this man is stable with established collaterals, and stenting first commits him to anticoagulation and can complicate subsequent biopsy access (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

options.text: Start empirical mediastinal radiotherapy while awaiting the histology
options.rationale: Empirical irradiation of the mediastinum destroys the diagnostic yield of subsequent biopsy and may deliver the wrong modality entirely if the tumour turns out to be chemosensitive (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online).

options.text: Commence therapeutic enoxaparin and repeat imaging in seven days
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is the near pair and is indicated when the obstruction is caused by catheter associated thrombus rather than extrinsic compression, which the imaging here does not show (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

explanation.summary: Superior vena caval obstruction was once treated as an emergency requiring immediate radiotherapy, but the modern approach separates the small group with true airway or neurological compromise from the majority who are stable with collateral flow. In the stable group, tissue diagnosis comes first because the histology dictates whether systemic therapy or radiotherapy is the primary modality. Around three quarters of cases are due to lung cancer, most commonly small cell, with lymphoma and germ cell tumours making up much of the remainder, and all three of those are chemosensitive. Intravascular thrombus around an indwelling device is the important non malignant cause and is managed with anticoagulation rather than irradiation.
key_points: Stridor, laryngeal oedema, reduced consciousness or haemodynamic compromise mark the group needing immediate intervention.
In stable patients, histology precedes treatment because it determines modality.
Corticosteroid before biopsy risks a non diagnostic specimen in lymphoma.
Endovascular stenting gives the fastest relief when symptoms are severe.
Catheter associated thrombus is the main non malignant cause and is treated with anticoagulation.
explanation.pearls: The chest wall collateral veins that make this diagnosis obvious take several weeks to develop, so their presence is itself reassurance that the obstruction has been gradual and that there is time to biopsy before treating.

subtopic_detail: Separating cold agglutinin disease from warm autoimmune haemolysis on the direct antiglobulin pattern
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 74 year old woman with six weeks of increasing tiredness. She tells you her fingers and the tip of her nose go a dusky blue and ache when she walks to the shops on a cold morning, and that the colour settles once she is back inside.

After one such walk last week she passed urine the colour of cola for a day. She has no joint pain, no rash and no recent infection. There is mild scleral icterus and no splenomegaly. The laboratory telephones to say the sample needed warming before the full blood count would run because the cells were clumping in the analyser.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 82 g/L (115-165), reticulocytes 145 x10^9/L (20-100), bilirubin 46 micromol/L (2-24), lactate dehydrogenase 480 U/L (120-250), haptoglobin less than 0.1 g/L (0.3-2.0)
data_table.Immunohaematology: Direct antiglobulin test positive for complement C3d, negative for immunoglobulin G

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: High dose prednisolone with a proton pump inhibitor and referral
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is first line in the near pair, warm autoimmune haemolysis, where the antiglobulin test is positive for immunoglobulin G and destruction is splenic; in the cold reactive form clearance is complement mediated and hepatic, and steroids are largely ineffective (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Elective splenectomy with pre operative vaccination and referral
options.rationale: Splenectomy helps when antibody coated cells are removed by splenic macrophages, but complement coated cells are cleared by Kupffer cells in the liver, so the operation removes the wrong organ (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin over two days with haematology referral
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin blocks Fc receptor mediated clearance and has little effect where complement drives destruction, and the response even in warm disease is brief and unreliable (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Therapeutic plasma exchange over five days with haematology referral
options.rationale: Exchange removes circulating antibody transiently and is reserved for fulminant haemolysis as a bridge, not as the management of a stable outpatient with a haemoglobin of 82 g/L (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Thermal protection with warmed transfusion and haematology referral
options.rationale: A direct antiglobulin test positive for complement alone, with cold triggered acrocyanosis and in vitro red cell clumping, identifies a cold reactive antibody, and the first line measures are avoidance of cold exposure and use of a blood warmer if transfusion is needed, with specialist assessment for an underlying lymphoproliferative clone (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia divides on the thermal amplitude of the antibody, and the direct antiglobulin pattern is what makes the split: immunoglobulin G with or without complement indicates a warm antibody, while complement alone indicates a cold one. That distinction changes treatment completely, because warm disease responds to corticosteroid and splenectomy while cold disease does not. Primary cold agglutinin disease is now recognised as a low grade clonal bone marrow lymphoproliferative disorder, which is why B cell directed therapy with rituximab, with or without a plasma cell or complement directed agent, has become the treatment of choice when transfusion dependence or symptoms demand it. Secondary cold agglutinins follow mycoplasma pneumonia or Epstein Barr virus infection and are usually self limiting.
key_points: Complement only positivity on the direct antiglobulin test indicates a cold reactive antibody.
Red cell clumping at room temperature causes a spuriously high mean cell volume and a spuriously low red cell count.
Corticosteroid and splenectomy are effective in warm disease but not in cold disease.
Cold avoidance and a blood warmer for transfusion are the immediate measures.
Primary disease reflects a marrow B cell clone and responds to rituximab based therapy.
explanation.pearls: Warming the sample to 37 degrees Celsius before running it corrects the clumping artefact, so a mean cell volume above 120 fL that normalises on a warmed repeat is a laboratory clue to the diagnosis before any antiglobulin test is back.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand
